title.text: Your first Python: variables, lists and error messages, next to the spreadsheet

objects.text: What does the same price-list task look like in Excel and in Python, and how do you read an error message when Python stops?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 5 of 24  |  Module B: Python for data
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. For four sessions you thought with data in a spreadsheet. Today you write your first lines of Python, and every idea arrives next to the spreadsheet thing you already know. We build a small Lakeside Mart price list, make mistakes on purpose, and learn to read what Python says back.

Nobody writes code without seeing errors, so reading them is the main skill of the day.

By the end of today you can run and save a notebook in Google Colab, and store values in variables. You can say what data type each value has: int, float, str or bool. You can keep many values in a list or in a dictionary, and look one up.

And you can read an error message from its last line, name the exception, and fix it. You will do all of it on the Lakeside Mart price list, with the spreadsheet answer beside every Python answer.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first,
then a Python notebook lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and plain words first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 4 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with laptops closed, so you can watch the pictures and ask questions. After a ten minute break you open a Google Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab.

For every task you predict, run, read the output and change one thing. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  You drew 200 samples of 30 orders and the 200 averages were not all the same. What is that variation called?
2.  A survey asks only the customers who come to the till on a Saturday. What goes wrong?
3.  Branch footfall and orders rise together. Does that show footfall causes orders?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 4. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. You drew 200 samples of 30 orders and the 200 averages were not all the same. What is that variation called?

A good answer is this. Sampling variability. Its size is the standard error, and it gets smaller when each sample is bigger.

Question two. A survey asks only the customers who come to the till on a Saturday. What goes wrong?

A good answer is this. Selection bias. Shoppers who never come on a Saturday are left out, so the sample does not stand for all customers.

Question three. Branch footfall and orders rise together. Does that show footfall causes orders?

A good answer is this. No. Correlation is not causation. A confounder such as branch size can lift both.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 4

rows.text: You drew 200 samples of 30 orders and the 200 averages were not all the same. What is that variation called?
Sampling variability. Its size is the standard error, and it gets smaller when each sample is bigger.
A survey asks only the customers who come to the till on a Saturday. What goes wrong?
Selection bias. Shoppers who never come on a Saturday are left out, so the sample does not stand for all customers.
Branch footfall and orders rise together. Does that show footfall causes orders?
No. Correlation is not causation. A confounder such as branch size can lift both.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. The two hundred averages differed because every sample holds different orders. That variation is sampling variability, and its size is the standard error. A survey of Saturday shoppers only is selection bias, because the shoppers who never come on a Saturday are left out.

And footfall and orders rising together is a correlation. It does not show cause, because a confounder such as branch size can lift both. Which of the three did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A name that stands for a stored value, like a named cell in Excel. In Python you choose the name, such as price_p001. In Session 2 a variable was a column of a table. Here it is a name that holds a value.
How Python stores a value: a whole number, a decimal number, text (a string) or True or False.
Values in order inside square brackets. Each has an index, and the first index is 0. It is like one column of a sheet.
Values stored under labels called keys. You look a value up by its key, as VLOOKUP does.
The error Python raises when a line cannot run. The traceback is its report. Its last line names the exception.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.70.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_tag_0.66.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_grid_0.66.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_key_0.66.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Variable (assignment). A name that stands for a stored value, like a named cell in Excel. In Python you choose the name, such as price_p001. In Session 2 a variable was a column of a table. Here it is a name that holds a value.

Data type (int, float, str, bool). How Python stores a value: a whole number, a decimal number, text (a string) or True or False.

List. Values in order inside square brackets. Each has an index, and the first index is 0. It is like one column of a sheet.

Dictionary (key-value pairs). Values stored under labels called keys. You look a value up by its key, as VLOOKUP does.

Exception (traceback). The error Python raises when a line cannot run. The traceback is its report. Its last line names the exception.

title.text:
A notebook mixes text cells and code
cells, and runs them from the top

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_notebook_11.90x4.25_4bd04a72.png
objects.alt: A notebook mixes text cells and code cells, and runs them from the top

objects.text: A Jupyter notebook is a document of cells. Colab runs it in a browser. The kernel is its engine.

slides.notes:
This is a notebook. A notebook is a Jupyter document made of cells, and Google Colab lets you open one in your browser, free, with nothing to install. A text cell holds headings and notes for people, and Python skips it. A code cell holds Python. You press the play button on its left, and the output appears directly under the cell.

Behind the notebook sits the kernel, the Python engine that remembers what you stored. Cells run in the order you press play, so a later cell can use what an earlier cell stored. Have you used a notebook before?

title.text:
Run the cells from the top,
and save a copy to Drive

objects.text: Three habits keep a notebook honest.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_notebook_0.70.png

objects.text: Cells run in the order you press play. A later cell uses only what an earlier one stored.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_gear_0.70.png

objects.text: If it goes odd, restart and run all cells from the top.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.70.png

objects.text: Save a copy in Drive. An idle session ends.

slides.notes:
Three habits will save you hours. One, cells run in the order you press play. If a cell uses a name that an earlier cell never created, Python tells you. Two, when the notebook behaves oddly, restart the session from the Runtime menu and run all the cells again from the top.

If it works from the top, it is trustworthy. Three, save a copy in Drive. A Colab session that sits idle ends, and everything in memory goes with it. Which of these habits do you already have from Excel?

title.text:
A variable is a name you give to a
stored value, like a named cell in Excel

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_sheetpy_7.70x4.80_9c400ab6.png
objects.alt: A variable is a name you give to a stored value, like a named cell in Excel

objects.text: Variable: a name that stands for a stored value.

runs.text: Sheet: the value sits in cell B2, which you could name Price. Python: it is stored under the name price_p001.
In Session 2 a variable was a column of a table. In programming a variable is a name that holds a value.

slides.notes:
Here is a sum you could do in your sleep: 12 units of product P001, at 3,200 shillings each. On the left is the spreadsheet. On the right is Python. In the sheet the price sits in cell B2, which you could give a name such as Price.

In Python it is stored under a name you choose. That name is a variable: a name that stands for a stored value. In Session 2 a variable meant a column of a table, so this is a second meaning of the word, and context tells you which.

The formula multiplies the two names, just as B4 multiplies B2 and B3, and the answer is 38,400. A name tells the reader what the number means, and B2 cannot. Which names would you choose for a loan amount and a term?

title.text:
Assignment works out the right side first,
then stores the answer under the name

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_assign_7.70x4.80_5541f427.png
objects.alt: Assignment works out the right side first, then stores the answer under the name

objects.text: Assignment: the equals sign stores a value under a name.

runs.text: Names use letters, digits and underscores. Case matters.
One equals sign stores. Two, ==, compare.
print() shows a value.

slides.notes:
This picture shows the third line of the first cell. The two boxes on the left hold what we already stored, each with its name and its data type, int. Python first works out the right side of the equals sign, which is the price times the quantity.

Then it stores the answer under the name on the left, line total. So the equals sign stores a value under a name. To ask a question you use two equals signs. Names have rules: letters, digits and underscores, with no spaces. What would happen if you wrote the name with a space?

title.text: Every value has a data type: int, float, str or bool

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_types_11.90x4.25_943c8a62.png
objects.alt: Every value has a data type: int, float, str or bool

objects.text: type() asks Python for a value's data type: how it is stored, as in Session 2.

slides.notes:
Every value has a data type, which is how Python stores it. An int is a whole number, like the price 3,200. A float is a decimal number, like the mean price 6720.0. A str, short for string, is text in quotes, like the product name Staples item 001.

And a bool is True or False, like the answer to the question: is the price above five thousand?

Here it is False. The function type tells you which kind a value is. This is the same data type idea from Session 2, now in code. Which type would you give a phone number?

title.text:
Python does the arithmetic
you know, plus a few new signs

rows.text: Multiply. Plus, minus and divide work as in Excel.
Divide. The answer is always a float.
Floor division: the whole part only.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.50.png

objects.text: prices is the list of five prices from the next slides. Floor division and remainder come back in Session 6, when we turn spend into loyalty points.

slides.notes:
Python does the arithmetic you already know. Multiply with a star, divide with a slash. Dividing always gives a float, so the mean of the five prices is 6720.0. Two new signs matter. Double slash is floor division: it keeps the whole part only, so 38,400 divided by a thousand gives 38.

In Session 6 that gives loyalty points. Percent gives the remainder, and double star is a power. Excel has the same ideas under other names, such as INT and MOD. Which of these would you have used in a formula last month?

title.text:
Quotes turn a number into a string,
and plus then joins instead of adding

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_trap_7.70x4.80_f40d21eb.png
objects.alt: Quotes turn a number into a string, and plus then joins instead of adding

objects.text: String (str): text inside quotes. A number in quotes is text.

runs.text: Plus on ints adds. Plus on strings joins.
int() or float() converts a string: type conversion (casting).
Check type() when a total looks odd.

slides.notes:
Here is the trap that catches everyone once. Without quotes, 3200 plus 8400 is 11600. With quotes, the same plus sign joins the two strings into '32008400'. Python raises no error, because joining two strings is perfectly legal. The answer is simply wrong. The cure is type conversion, also called casting: int turns a string into a whole number, and float turns it into a decimal number.

Whenever a total looks odd, ask Python for the data type first. Where might numbers arrive as text in your own work?

title.text:
A list holds values in order, and
the first position is index 0

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_list_7.70x4.80_0e85da5a.png
objects.alt: A list holds values in order, and the first position is index 0

objects.text: List: values in order, inside square brackets.

runs.text: A list is like one column of a sheet.
Index: the position of an item, counting from 0.
len, sum and max work on the whole list.

slides.notes:
A list is Python's version of one column of a sheet. This list is called prices, and it holds the first five Lakeside prices: 3,200, 8,400, 8,700, 7,000, 6,300. The numbers below the cells are the index, the position of each item. The index starts at zero, not one, which surprises everyone at first.

So prices with a zero in square brackets is the first item, 3,200. The function len tells you how many items there are: 5. Why do you think programmers count from zero?

slides.notes:
Here is the list at work, with the Excel formula beside each step. Len counts the items, like COUNT: 5. Sum adds them, like SUM: 33,600. Max gives the largest, 8,700, and min the smallest, 3,200. The mean is the sum divided by the length, 6720.0, and it is a float.

And append adds one item at the end of the list, as typing the next price in a new cell would. Each function has a Python name and an Excel name, but the idea is the same. Which Excel function would you reach for to find the second largest price?

title.text:
A dictionary stores key-value pairs,
so you find a value by its label

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_dict_7.70x4.80_4e4e555e.png
objects.alt: A dictionary stores key-value pairs, so you find a value by its label

objects.text: Dictionary: values stored under labels called keys.

runs.text: Each key is paired with one value: a key-value pair.
Curly brackets hold the pairs.
You ask by key, so the order does not matter.

slides.notes:
A dictionary stores key-value pairs. The keys on the left are the product codes. The values on the right are the prices. To find one you ask by key: the price for P003 is 8,700. In Excel you do the same lookup with VLOOKUP, a table, and a column number.

A dictionary does it with the key alone. Curly brackets hold the pairs, and each key can appear only once. You will use dictionaries for every lookup table in this course. What other lookup tables do you keep in Excel?

title.text:
List or dictionary: choose by
how you will look things up

objects.text: List

runs.text: Values in order.
Find an item by its index: 0, 1, 2.
Excel twin: one column to add up.

objects.text: Dictionary

runs.text: Values with labels.
Find an item by its key, such as 'P003'.
Excel twin: a VLOOKUP table, for a lookup.

objects.text: Ask first: will I find it by position or by label?

slides.notes:
How do you choose between the two?

Ask how you will look the value up. A list is ordered, and you find an item by its index, so it suits one column of values that you add up or average. A dictionary has labels, and you find an item by its key, so it suits a lookup table such as a price list.

If you would write a VLOOKUP in Excel, you want a dictionary. If you would write a SUM over a column, you want a list. Which would you use for the loan amounts of one branch?

title.text:
A traceback is the report of a
failure: read its last line first

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_traceback_11.90x4.25_a1581fe1.png
objects.alt: A traceback is the report of a failure: read its last line first

objects.text: From a real run. Colab adds colours and an arrow. The last line is the same.

slides.notes:
When a line cannot run, Python raises an exception and prints a traceback, a report of where it failed. Here I misspelt price as prise. Read the last line first. It names the exception, NameError, and gives a message: name 'prise_p001' is not defined. Python has nothing stored under that name, so it is a spelling slip or a cell you have not run.

The lines above it tell you where: the cell, the line number, and the line of code that failed. Beginners read from the top and get lost. Read from the bottom. What would you check first for a NameError?

title.text: Five exceptions cover most beginner errors

rows.text: No variable has that name: a spelling slip, or its cell has not run.
Check the spelling. Run the earlier cell.
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'
An operation met the wrong data type, such as int plus str.
The dictionary has no such key.
Check the key spelling and its quotes.
IndexError: list index out of range
The list has no item at that index.
The last index is len minus 1.
The line breaks a grammar rule.

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_grid_0.50.png

objects.text: Messages copied from real runs in Python 3.10 or later. Newer Python versions may word a message slightly differently.

slides.notes:
Five exceptions will account for most of your errors this week. NameError: the name does not exist. TypeError: an operation met the wrong data type, such as an int and a string. KeyError: the dictionary has no such key. IndexError: the list has no item at that position.

And SyntaxError: the line breaks the grammar of Python, usually a bracket or quote that was never closed. Each message on the slide is copied from a real run. The wording can differ a little between Python versions, but the exception name does not. Which of the five do you expect to meet first?

title.text: Four steps read any error and fix it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_0b37e0d2.png
objects.alt: Four steps read any error and fix it

objects.text: Change one thing at a time. An error is information.

slides.notes:
Here are the four steps I would like you to follow every time. One, read the last line. Two, find the line number in the traceback. Three, name the cause: is it a spelling slip, a wrong data type, or a wrong position?

Four, fix one thing and run the cell again, from the top if the notebook has grown. Do not change three things at once, because then you cannot tell which one fixed it. An error message is information. It is Python telling you exactly where it got stuck.

What do you usually do first when Excel shows an error?

title.text:
A quarter of the raw export stores the
price as text, so Python needs a conversion

objects.text: 10,345 of the 41,259 rows in orders_raw.csv hold unit_price as text such as UGX 7,800. Python cannot add text until you clean it.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_a3aeeeb9.png
objects.alt: A quarter of the raw export stores the price as text, so Python needs a conversion

slides.notes:
This is the same trap on real data. In the raw order line export, 10,345 of 41,259 rows store the unit price as text, with the letters UGX in front and a comma inside, like UGX 7,800. That is about 25 in every 100 rows. Python will not add those values, because they are strings.

Calling int on one raises a ValueError, and the last line reads: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'UGX 7,800'. Cleaning it is the work of Session 8, and today you learn to recognise the problem from the data type. Which column in your own files might be stored as text?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: The cell that creates the name has not run, or the spelling differs.
Run the cells from the top. Match the spelling and the capital letters.
TypeError on a sum or a plus
A string is mixed with a number.
Convert it with int() or float(). Check the quotes.
The key is missing from the dictionary, or it is not a string.
A bracket or a quote was not closed.
Count the opening and closing signs on the line.
NOT YET after your answer is right
The cell was run before the answer was typed, or the name differs.
Run the answer cell again, then the check line.

slides.notes:
Five messages you may meet. A NameError means the cell that creates the name has not run, or the spelling differs, including the capital letters. A TypeError on a sum means a string is mixed with a number, so convert it. A KeyError means the key is missing from the dictionary.

Check the quotes, because the keys are strings. A SyntaxError about a bracket means something was never closed. And NOT YET after a right answer usually means the cell ran before you typed the answer. Read the last line first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: Two prices are typed in quotes. What does '3200' + '8400' give, and why?
'32008400'. Both values are strings, so plus joins them. Convert with int() to add.
A dictionary has no key P099. What does the last line of the error say, and what is the exception?
KeyError: 'P099'. The exception is a KeyError.
How many items does a list of five prices have, and what is the index of the last one?
Five items. The last index is 4, because counting starts at 0.
